Meringue is a light, sweet, white, foamy mixture made by beating egg whites with sugar until the mixture becomes thick, glossy, and holds its shape. It is used widely in baking and dessert-making.

To understand meringue, picture what happens when you whip egg whites vigorously. The liquid egg whites trap millions of tiny air bubbles and transform into a stiff, white foam — almost like shaving cream, but made of eggs. When you add sugar to this and keep beating, the sugar stabilizes that foam, making it smooth, glossy, and strong enough to hold a shape. That final mixture — airy, white, and sweet — is meringue.

So meringue is a stable foam of air trapped in egg whites and held together by sugar. It is almost weightless, because most of its volume is just air.
What it looks, feels, and tastes like

• Before baking: Thick, glossy, brilliant white, and soft — almost like very stiff whipped cream.
  • After baking: The outside becomes crisp and dry, like a light shell, while the inside can remain slightly soft and chewy, similar to a marshmallow. The colour turns from pure white to a pale ivory or light golden-brown.
  • Taste: Very sweet, clean, and delicate. It melts gently on the tongue. It has almost no flavour beyond sweetness and a faint egginess.
  • Texture in the mouth: Baked meringue tends to be airy and crisp, crumbling or dissolving easily as you eat it.

Meringue isn't just one fixed thing — chefs make it in three different ways, and each produces a slightly different result. You'll encounter these terms if you read baking recipes or food writing:

1. French meringue (the basic, everyday kind)
Raw egg whites are beaten with fine sugar until stiff and glossy. This is the simplest version to make, but it is also the most fragile — it must be baked soon after making. This is what most people at home make.

2. Swiss meringue (the smooth, silky kind)
The egg whites and sugar are gently warmed together in a bowl placed over simmering water, whisked the entire time, and then beaten into a thick, glossy foam. The gentle heat makes it more stable and gives it a smoother, denser texture than French meringue.

3. Italian meringue (the cooked, very stable kind)
Very hot sugar syrup — cooked to a precise temperature — is poured in a thin stream into egg whites that are already being beaten. The heat from the syrup partially cooks the egg whites, making this the most stable and safest type (since it's already been heated). Professional bakers and pastry chefs favour it for toppings and fillings because it holds its shape beautifully and won't deflate easily.
How meringue is used in cooking and baking

Meringue plays several distinct roles in the kitchen:

As a topping: Perhaps the most iconic use is on top of lemon meringue pie, where soft peaks of meringue are spread over a lemon custard filling, then briefly baked or torched until the surface turns golden-brown with slightly charred tips. The contrast between the tangy filling and the sweet, soft meringue is the point of the dish.

As baked cookies or shells: Meringue can be piped or spooned into small mounds on a baking tray and baked very slowly at a low temperature until completely dry and crisp all the way through. These are called meringues (the small baked pieces) or meringue cookies. They are very light, crisp, and sweet.

As the base of Pavlova: Pavlova is a famous dessert made from a large round of meringue baked so that the outside is crisp but the inside stays soft and marshmallow-like. It is then topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit. Pavlova is named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova and is especially popular in Australia and New Zealand.

As a component in other desserts: Meringue is also an ingredient inside many other preparations — folded into mousses to make them light and airy, used as the filling in macarons (the delicate French sandwich cookies), spread over ice cream in Baked Alaska (a spectacular dessert where ice cream is covered in meringue and then briefly baked or torched so the outside browns while the ice cream stays frozen inside), and mixed into various buttercreams to create a light, silky cake frosting.
A critical property: meringue and moisture

One essential thing to know about meringue is that it is extremely sensitive to humidity and moisture. Sugar naturally attracts water from the surrounding air. Because meringue contains so much sugar, it readily absorbs moisture — and when it does, it softens, becomes sticky, or starts to "weep" (tiny drops of liquid form on its surface). This is why:

  • Meringue is best made on a dry day, not a humid one.
  • Baked meringues go soft if stored improperly or left out in a humid environment.
  • Lemon meringue pie often needs to be eaten the same day, because the moisture from the filling and the air gradually makes the meringue layer weep and soften.
How the word is used in sentences

The noun "meringue" works in two slightly different ways:

  • As an uncountable noun (referring to the substance or mixture itself): "She spread a thick layer of meringue over the pie." / "The recipe calls for meringue made with three egg whites."
  • As a countable noun (referring to an individual baked meringue piece): "He ate two meringues from the bakery." / "She decorated the cake with small meringues."

When you see "a meringue" or "meringues" (plural), it almost always refers to the individual baked pieces — the cookies or shells. When you see "meringue" without an article, it usually refers to the mixture or the concept.

Meringue is a delicate, airy, sweet preparation made from beaten egg whites and sugar. It can be soft and cloud-like, used as a topping; crisp and dry, eaten as a cookie; or marshmallow-soft inside a baked shell. It appears in a remarkable range of desserts — from pies to cakes to standalone sweets — and is one of the fundamental building blocks of Western baking and pastry-making. Its defining qualities are its lightness (because it is mostly air), its whiteness, its sweetness, and its fragility in the face of moisture.
